claims.text: The initial alloy is an as-cast, equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr alloy.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has excellent mechanical properties at room temperature and 1000 °C.
Partial substitution of Hf by Sc will reduce the alloy density.
Partial substitution of Hf by Sc will preserve a single-phase BCC structure.
The Sc-modified alloy will retain the high strength of HfMoTaTiZr at room temperature.
The Sc-modified alloy will retain the high strength of HfMoTaTiZr at approximately 1000 °C.
Substitutional incorporation of Sc will produce slight lattice-parameter shifts.
Preserving the BCC solid solution will maintain beneficial dislocation-strengthening features.
Sc has a significantly lower atomic mass than Hf.
Replacing Hf with lower-atomic-mass Sc lowers the overall alloy density.
Solid-solution strengthening is the main strengthening mechanism in the proposed single-phase alloy.
Strengthening will be maintained if phase stability and lattice distortion remain similar to those of the baseline alloy.
The Sc-modified alloy will retain creep resistance comparable to the baseline at approximately 1000 °C.
An inert or vacuum environment avoids oxidation during high-temperature mechanical testing.

contradictions.description: The experimental series explicitly includes x = 0, but the rejection rule falsifies the hypothesis if any tested composition reduces density by less than about 5%. The x = 0 baseline necessarily has zero density reduction relative to itself, so the experiment is self-falsifying.

The intervention proposes finding or optimizing a successful Sc content, whereas the rejection rule treats failure of any individual composition as falsification. A poorly performing composition would therefore reject the optimization hypothesis even if another tested Sc content met all targets.
